posts.name: Ethan Mollick
posts.text:
I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. 

On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base.

Here is a fun example:  "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end"

Astra Max in Codex: https://t.co/lyalJY4E4g 
5.1 Max in Code: https://t.co/WNt4lA05B6
Argon in Antigravity: https://t.co/7gUAuCA49J
posts.text_ja:
発表前にGemini 4をそれなりの時間試してみました。全体として、Gemini 4は従来のGeminiモデルから大きく進歩しており、Fable/Mythos/Astraの基準をクリアした初のOpenAI・Anthropic以外のモデルです。また、Gemini 3シリーズによくあった奇妙な人格面の問題がなくなり、従来のGeminiモデルより格段に快適で、よりエージェント的になっています。実は大きな強みとして、ClaudeやAstraとは非常に異なる人格とセンスを持っているため、AIの世界に良い追加になると感じました。

実用性の面では、一部の分野ではOpenAIやAnthropicと少なくとも同等です（非常に創造的で良い書き手です）。一方で、複雑なマルチエージェント作業を含め、遅れている分野もあります。結論を断定しすぎる傾向があり、少し怠け気味なところもあります。これにはAntigravityのハーネスが競合ほど優れていないことも影響していると思います。それでも、Gemini 4をベースにすれば、モデル能力は急速に向上すると期待しています。

面白い例を one つ紹介します：「究極のブルータリズム都市ビルダーを作って。遊びたいだけの人には直感的で楽しい建物の操作を多数用意しつつ、奥深く洗練された操作も、ゲームをよく知る人には用意してほしい」

posts.name: Anthropic
posts.text:
New on our Engineering blog: Creating in-house source control. 

In May, we merged around 2,500 code changes per day. In September, we merged more than 30,000 per day. As a result, we became bottlenecked by developer infrastructure built for human (rather than agent) scale.  

Here, we share how we built a new version control system—and fully migrated our monorepo from git—in five months: https://t.co/wzNkwHs7IN

clusters.title: Alibabaが強化学習基盤「QwenGyre」を発表
clusters.summary: Alibaba公式アカウント「Qwen」が、超長期のエージェント（AIが複数手順の作業を自律的に進める仕組み）学習向けの強化学習基盤「QwenGyre」を発表した。GPU割り当てを動的に変える仕組みや、学習データを整理する仕組みを備えるとしている。投稿では、Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95Bでの検証結果として、NL2RepoBenchのスコア向上や学習時間の短縮が挙げられている。

posts.name: Qwen
posts.text:
Introducing QwenGyre, bringing elastic RL to extreme-long-horizon (XLong) agent training. ✨

It launches with two core designs: 🥳
- Elastic Scheduler: reallocates GPUs between rollout & training as demand shifts—live executions never interrupted. Up to 1.85× speedup over Colocate, 1.78× over Async.
- Trajectory Processor: turns branching executions (compaction, sub-agents, retries) into prefix-shared trajectory trees with bounded, deduplicated training samples. Partial progress after timeout still gets scored.

Scaled to Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B with ~700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre lifts NL2RepoBench from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps, cutting end-to-end training time by ~44% vs Async.

posts.name: Sakana AI
posts.text:
Introducing Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS): Recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence

Blog: https://t.co/LkQe5k7jOW

As AI systems tackle increasingly open-ended research problems, human experts may struggle to assess results and guide further progress. The model itself may be the best available optimizer and evaluator. The challenge is obtaining useful self-supervision within that homogeneous loop, where a model risks reinforcing its own blind spots rather than correcting them.

We ask whether a model can learn from the collective intelligence of its own team.

We introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS). One shared model solves tasks through a team of virtual subagents, searches for better multi-agent workflows, then uses its own judgments to select the best ones.

Training on the best team’s executions provides self-supervision by distilling the team’s collective experience into the shared model.

We ran two cycles using a 27B open-weights model on synthetic open-ended research tasks. After the second cycle, score per output token reached 1.2-1.6x the base model's level across four research benchmarks.

Three key results:

First, MASS enables role generalization within an RSI loop: training only on task-solving data from the optimizee naturally improves the capabilities of both the optimizer and the evaluator.

Second, multi-agent trajectories are more efficient training data than single-agent trajectories for RSI.

Third, optimizer capacity, rather than evaluator capacity, can be the bottleneck in the speed of improvement.

We believe the community needs to investigate homogeneous RSI carefully to support AI safety. When a model is also its own evaluator, shared blind spots could allow mistakes to be accepted as progress and reinforced through training. For AI to improve beyond human expertise safely, we need to understand these failures and preserve effective ways to detect them and intervene.

Paper: https://t.co/SzXDlAzrUO
Code: https://t.co/xc870ZHRgh

This work was a collaboration with researchers at UC Berkeley.

clusters.title: Karpathy氏、LLMの普及に大きな認識差があると指摘
clusters.summary: 【意見】AI研究者のAndrej Karpathy氏は、LLMの能力に対する社会の認識の差が広がっていると述べた。概算として、約60億人（人口の約75%）はLLMにほとんど触れていないとし、約10〜20億人は無料版のチャットAIを時々使う程度だと書いた。Wharton教授のEthan Mollick氏は、先端モデルにアクセスできる研究所の約5,000人の多くも、その能力を十分に使えていないと指摘した。

posts.name: Andrej Karpathy
posts.text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

- ざっくり計算すると、約60億人（人口の約75%）はLLMにほとんど触れたことがありません。

Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems you really care about.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

authors.role: AI論文紹介メディア「AIDB」運営

posts.name: AIDB
posts.text:
AIを使っても非エンジニアとエンジニアでは思い通りに物を作る能力に大きな隔たりがあることが示されています。
実験ではエンジニアが頼んだときの要求達成率が78%、コードを読めない人のときが23%でした。
ただし、AIがあいまいなリクエストを先に質問して明確にしていくと、大きく改善されるそうです。
例えば「不明点を先に質問して」と指示しておくことが推奨されます。

実験では、13のAIエージェントに、何段階も続く開発作業を任せました。
ユーザーは、実際の利用記録から作った4種類の人物（エンジニア、新人開発者、プロダクト担当、コードを読めない人）をシミュレートしています。

コードを読めない人の頼み方は、症状だけをぼんやり伝える、自分でも要望がはっきりしない、ときには壊してしまう指示を出す、となりがち。
AIがそれを確かめずにそのまま実行すると、何往復しても要求に届きません。

そこで大事になるのが、作り始める前に不明点をつぶすこと。
研究者らはこれを「正しく聞く」と呼び、「正しく見つける（直すべき場所を探す）」「正しく直す」と合わせて、AIがコードを読めない人と働くための3つの力として挙げています。

posts.name: AIDB
posts.text:
弱いAIに強いAIが書いた「教科書（文章ベース）」を読ませるだけで弱いAIの実力が爆発的に伸びる可能性が示唆されています。
中国の西湖大学の研究者らによる報告。

やり方はこうです。
1. 強いAIは解けて弱いAIは解けない問題を集める
2. 弱いAIが解く
3. 別の役が「何が足りないか」を診断して教え方を決める
4. 強いAIが手本を示す
5. まとめ役が教科書に書き足す
モデルの重みは一切いじりません。

実験では、DeepSeek V4 Proが書いた教科書でDeepSeek V4 Flashの数学が27.6%から51.7%、GPU向けプログラムの生成が9.4%から48.6%に上がりました。
なお、別のファミリーモデル（Qwen）に渡しても有効でした。

研究者らは「強いAIのノウハウを別のAIに渡せる」ことの実証と位置づけています。

なお、今回試したのは数学とGPUプログラム生成の2つだけなので、ほかの仕事でも同じように効くかはまだ分かりません。

posts.text:
AIエージェントはもはや生態学的に捉えて対策する必要があり、恐るべき特徴は「協力できる」という点。
エージェント集団は"ある数"を超えると集団としての能力は強力になり、さらに一気に自己増殖する力を持つとのこと。
ハーバード大学・NTT Researchの田中氏らによる報告です。

現実的に想定されるのは以下のような流れです。
①エージェントがコンピュータに侵入し、こっそり自分の分身を配置する
②サーバー内のエージェント集団が徐々に大きくなる
③あるタイミングで侵入の技術が向上し、さらに増える。

一定数を下回ると絶滅し上回ると爆発的に増えるという、動物の「アリー効果」と似ているようです。

そのため、少数のエージェントをテストして安全でも、大きな集団の安全は保証できません。
集団を少しずつ大きくしながら能力の伸びを測り、境目の数を見積もる必要があるとのことです。

authors.name: Nathan Lambert
authors.role: Trillium Labs創設者・オープンモデル

posts.name: Nathan Lambert
posts.text:
This is the best piece I’ve read to date on the Chinese data economy for LLMs, and how it compares to the US counterparts (summarized by Mercor, Surge, and Handshake having the biggest network, SUPPLY, but also many companies with specialized services, in the form of RL-ready environments). China’s leading spenders, Tencent, Alibaba, and ByteDance, don’t mirror OpenAI and Anthropic leading the US market.

The Chinese market likely has a bias similar to their “ownership” mentality of more LLM builders in house, like Meituan, RedNote, and Xiaomi, whereas major US tech services build more on APIs and existing open-weight models.

Altogether, it seems like Chinese labs were 6–12 months behind on willingness to spend on data, relative to the US, but are rapidly catching up.

I've been hearing lots of murmurings on China's AI industry, but folks are secretive, so it's hard to put this all together.
posts.text_ja:
中国のLLM向けデータ経済と、それが米国の同業他社とどう比較されるかについて、これまで読んだ中で最良の記事です(Mercor、Surge、Handshakeが最大のネットワーク「SUPPLY」を持ち、さらにRL対応の環境を特化型サービスとして提供する企業も多い、という要約)。中国の主要支出企業であるTencent、Alibaba、ByteDanceは、米国市場でOpenAIやAnthropicが占めるような構図とは一致しません。

中国市場には、Meituan、RedNote、Xiaomiのように多くのLLMを社内で開発する「自社保有」志向と似た偏りがあるとみられます。一方、米国の主要テック企業はAPIや既存のオープンウェイトモデルを基に構築することが多いです。

全体として、中国のラボは6〜12か月ほど遅れている、と見られます。
